doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 2, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Cutting a European tour short as the Covid ban hit, March 2020
summary: Having played constantly for 32 years, she describes her March tour, the Europe flight ban, cancelling gigs and flying home via Heathrow with the Brubeck Brothers.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So you are a person who for years has played almost constantly, at least from what I can see.
I didn’t realize that until the pandemic. Yes I’ve played constantly for 32 years.
Was there — sometimes you hear the term, “I had an aha moment.” And I wonder if you had an “Uh oh” moment when cancellations started to come in. Did they come all in at once?

Actually it was very stressful because I had just started a tour. I started the tour on March 1, and I was working January and February in the States. So we did the jazz cruise, we came home, went to San Diego came home, went to Florida came home. So I had a pretty full January and February and actually a pretty full year booked you know. Some of the tours I do in Europe are organized two years in advance. So this particular one in March was two years in the making, which is a lot of phone calls, a lot of emails, a lot of work, Not necessarily for me but for the European musicians who organize them. So it was going to be a very busy five weeks but all great gigs, I was really looking forward to it. We got to about March — we got to my birthday, which was March 9, and we had a little party. It was a night off, and we had a little party in Germany and it was getting really strange then because these are people I’ve known for at least ten years and they all wanted to hang out with me and have coffee and cake and just hang out. And it was just like so weird because I couldn’t really be near them and it was just a strange situation back in March. And then some gigs were cancelling. Some gigs at the end of March were cancelling and I was like well I’ll probably go home sooner but I don’t know when. And then the Europe flight ban happened, which was a couple of days after my birthday, three days after the birthday, so like March 12 the Europe ban was announced. And Brian called me and said, “You’ve got to come home,” and I said, “I agree.” So even though

gigs next week and the week after weren’t cancelled, I cancelled them and they were not happy with me. In fact some of the contracts, some of the promoters were actually saying, “You owe us money.” You know what I mean? “You can’t cancel out of these gigs.” Of course the gig cancelled but I was just ahead, a day ahead even. And I felt bad because I left certain band leaders and promoters in the lurch. I was on the phone for three hours to United trying to get a flight home. I got one via Heathrow, because I thought well they haven’t banned in the U.K. yet, if I have to be overnight in the U.K. I can still get home to the States. And so I got a flight on the Friday which was the day after the Europe ban — well the day when it was going to get a lot harder to get back to the States. And I got one through Heathrow and I got on the plane at Heathrow and it was packed, and the Brubeck Brothers were on board because they had just finished a week at Ronnie Scott’s. And unfortunately I believe that Dan had a brief episode with Corona that was not pleasant at all, so that was sad. I was talking to Chris on the plane and his wife and they cancelled, that was a big year for them because it was the hundredth anniversary of Dave Brubeck and they had a lot of work in Europe booked and they were on the same flight.
We met them at the jazz convention in New Orleans, they were doing the Brubeck thing.
Yeah, Chris Brubeck actually lives in not far from here in Wilton, I believe near where Dave lived, Dave Brubeck. Super sweet guys. Great guys.
